Exterior siding and masonry work continue on new townhomes at the Riverbank, a housing development at the former White Eagle site in Niles. Victor Hilitski/For the Sun-Times SHARE COPY LINK Share CLOSE Twitter Facebook Bluesky Email Reddit Flipboard The largest development project in Niles is transforming what was once a mecca for Chicago’s Polish community into hundreds of new units of housing. Village officials said the Riverbank, a 10-building residential project at the former White Eagle Events and Convention Center, is expected to be finished in December 2027. The White Eagle — which cost $250,000 to demolish — was a staple among Polish families for funeral receptions, baptisms and other gatherings. The venue, at 6839 N. Milwaukee Ave., hosted dignitaries including former President Jimmy Carter, Pope John Paul II and Muhammad Ali. Poland’s former President Lech Wałesa also visited the White Eagle. It was across from St. Adalbert Cemetery, a Catholic — and largely Polish — burial site. Foundation rebar and excavation work continues at the Riverbank, a $156 million housing development project in Niles. Victor Hilitski/Victor Hilitski/For the Sun-Times Once the $156 million Riverbank project is complete, Niles officials said the gateway will be revitalized with art, much-needed housing and public green space. “What you’re going to see along Milwaukee Avenue is transformation,” Chris Ragusto, Niles’ director of community development, said. Developing the Riverbank is Noah Properties, led by Bart Przyjemski. Przyjemski is a native of Poland and a former Niles resident. He purchased the site in December 2025 for $5.7 million, with a $3.9 million mortgage from California-based Genesis Capital, property records show. The Riverbank will have 354 luxury units including studios, one-, two- and four-bedroom homes. Pricing hasn’t been determined. The site, spanning 7 acres, will also have a new park, public plaza, pool, playground and parking. Construction has been ongoing for the last six months, according to village officials. In July, developers hit a major milestone: framing for the six rows of townhomes was completed. Some of the first townhomes have their windows installed, with interior finishes underway. By the end of August, crews will begin installing drywall, tile and flooring in some of the first units. Steel framing is going up on one the apartment buildings, while a second apartment building has its foundation for the attached parking garage poured. Where the White Eagle used to sit is a giant excavated hole until construction starts at that portion of the site. The developer is awaiting on permit approvals for buildings planned at the front of the property. The medical building at 6759 N. Milwaukee has been vacated, and it will eventually be demolished. Niles Mayor George Alpogianis said the Riverbank will help usher in the next chapter for the site. The apartments and townhomes will attract young professionals and families, who may not be ready or have the money to buy a single-family home yet, but still want to be in Niles for its location, schools and public libraries, he said. Niles Mayor George Alpogianis speaks alongside village representatives, during a construction tour at the Riverbank development project. Victor Hilitski/For the Sun-Times There’s great demand for high-end luxury rental units in Niles, Alpogianis said. For example, Novu, a new luxury 180-unit apartment at 6633 N. Milwaukee that was developed by Noah Properties, is 80% leased. And the luxury apartment building the Grand Stone, at 9201 N. Milwaukee, leased all 48 of its units in one month, according to Ragusto. The White Eagle closed at the end of 2025. Ted Przybylo opened the business in 1947 and moved it from Chicago to Niles in 1967. The White Eagle’s nearly 60-year run was “so monumental” for Niles and those who frequented it, including much of Chicago’s Democratic Party, Alpogianis said. But there’s no longer a need for a roughly 1,000-seat banquet hall like the White Eagle. “As much as we worked with [the owners] to try and figure things out and try to reimagine the White Eagle, it unfortunately had its day,” Alpogianis said. The White Eagle site is one the village “wanted to pay particular attention to,” Ragusto said. Niles’ South Milwaukee Avenue Corridor Plan calls for widening Milwaukee Avenue, which Noah Properties will undertake, along with new landscaping and an art plaza. And the Niles 2040 Comprehensive Plan, adopted in 2024, calls for more places for residents to live, work, shop and play. Remembering the history of the White Eagle is important as the Milwaukee Avenue parcel evolves, officials said. The Niles Historical Society took a “number of items” from the banquet hall prior to demolition, Katie Schneider, deputy village manager of Niles, said. The items will likely be housed at the Niles Historical and Cultural Center, where they will help tell the story of Polish immigrants in the village. But it’s possible they will be repurposed on the property, along with stained glass and original cladding from the former Silver Leaf Tavern that once stood on the site. “The Polish community has just been such a part of our history, and that’s a large part because of the White Eagle,” Schneider said. “The bread and butter of Niles is our small businesses and people that come here to build and truly live the American dream. And they have family-owned businesses. That’s what the White Eagle really was.” Related Developer plans 354 apartments at White Eagle site in Niles White Eagle banquets in Niles to close at end of year SHARE COPY LINK Share CLOSE Twitter Facebook Bluesky Email Reddit Flipboard Abby Miller Chicago Sun-Times Money reporter, development Money Have a money question? News 1 d ago Rare 17th-century wall paintings restored at Lithuaniaâs Siesikai Castle News 1 d ago Lithuaniaâs Interior Ministry reports cyberattack on archived information system News 1 d ago Lithuania and Philippines agree to coordinate labour migration News 1 d ago PM urges Lithuanian banks to prepare for payments during national mobilisation News 1 d ago Suspect in Alytus football playerâs stabbing will not be charged due to insanity News 1 d ago EC says it is âcarefully assessingâ Baltic request for â¬500 million in drone defences News 1 d ago Lithuania launches largest annual mobilisation drills, tests wartime supply system News 1 d ago Lithuania signs cooperation deal with US defence tech firm Mach Industries News 1 d ago LRT English Newsletter: America is back, for now News 2 d ago Lithuania to let Belarusians apply for residence permits in Armenia, Georgia News 2 d ago Denmark issues warning over âlow but growing riskâ of limited Russian attack News 2 d ago Lithuanian PM suggests cutting public transport fares to offset fuel costs News 2 d ago Vilnius streetworks leave small businesses counting the cost â and struggling to survive News 2 d ago Lithuania sets date for next local elections News 2026.09.13 10:00 Middle powers guarding Europeâs eastern flank â opinion MK AR Maksym Khylko , Adam Reichardt, New Eastern Europe 2026.09.13 10:00 War in Ukraine | AP Ukraine and Poland, two Central and Eastern European states whose regional influence has often been underestimated, illustrate how middle powers can shape outcomes once reserved for great powers, Maksym Khylko and Adam Reichard write for the New Eastern Europe Magazine, partners of LRT English. In January 2026, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney used the podium of the World Economic Forum in Davos to warn that the world was living through âa rupture, not a transitionâ in the international order, in which great powers increasingly treat economic interdependence, tariffs and supply chains as instruments of coercion. His central claim â that middle powers are not powerless but must act together or risk being âon the menuâ rather than at the table â has become a reference point for a broader debate about the future of democracies in the changing world order. Scholars and analysts from Central and Eastern Europe have converged on a similar diagnosis. In a special 2026 edition of New Eastern Europe dedicated to this new disorder, Andreas Umland argues that the world as we know it is nearing its end and is increasingly being displaced by a system that presents itself openly as non-liberal, if not outright anti-liberal, reflecting the shifting preferences of powerful leaders. Wojciech Michnik links this trend to the fate of European security, arguing that the sense of Europe adrift in the emerging order stems from both external shocks and internal shortcomings: on the one side, the United States is signalling that Europe is no longer the central theatre of American strategy; on the other, Europeans themselves remain divided over how far they are willing to go in assuming strategic autonomy. Paul Bell frames the resulting predicament starkly, describing Europe as sandwiched between autocrats who, for their own distinct purposes, are each working to weaken it, undermine European policy and democratic values. The case for European strategic autonomy rests on a structural observation: no single EU member state, and arguably not the Union as a whole in its current institutional configuration, possesses the sovereign capability to guarantee its security, prosperity or technological relevance if the assumptions underlying transatlantic and global economic integration continue to erode. Discussing EU strategic autonomy as independence (disengagement from external dependence), as responsibility (binding more closely with like-minded partners to jointly resist coercion), and as hedging (preserving room for manoeuvre between rival powers), Daniel Fiott argues that the EUâs ability to resist being wedged apart by Washington or Beijing depends less on a top-down Brussels-led strategy than on internal binding efforts among member states. When considering the role of middle powers in this context, the Central and Eastern European states play key roles: Ukraineâs resistance to the Russian invasion has served as the external shock that pushed EU member states towards a more responsibility-oriented posture, while Poland has played an important role in anchoring the Unionâs defence posture around this model of autonomy, particularly at the initial stage of providing assistance to Ukraine and, in parallel, unprecedented investments in its own defence. Poland | AP Ukraine, Poland, and the EU: middle powers in practice The concept of the middle power has a long lineage in international relations theory, dating to debates at the founding of the United Nations, when Canadian and Australian diplomats sought recognition for states that, while lacking great-power capability, made disproportionate contributions to the war effort and collective security architecture. A middle power is generally understood as a state occupying an intermediate position in the international hierarchy: it lacks the capacity of a great power to determine systemic outcomes unilaterally, but possesses sufficient economic, military, diplomatic or normative resources to shape outcomes within a region or issue-area, typically through coalition-building and multilateralism rather than coercion. Eduard Jordaanâs influential distinction between âtraditionalâ middle powers â wealthy and stable democratic states, which tend to legitimise the existing order â and âemergingâ middle powers, which are often semi-peripheral, more assertive regionally, and less committed to defending a status quo that historically marginalised them, remains analytically useful today. This distinction helps to comprehend the phenomenon of the rise of authoritarian and illiberal middle powers, in particular in the Middle East and Asia, which combine regional assertiveness with a transactional, sovereigntist posture toward international institutions. Thus, the challenge facing the EU is not simply that great powers behave without constraint, but that the âmiddle tierâ of the international system, once assumed to be a natural constituency for a rules-based order, is itself becoming ideologically heterogeneous and, in some cases, corrosive of that order. Against this backdrop, it is in the EUâs vital interest to support the development and cooperation of democratically-oriented middle powers. Ukraine and Poland are critical cases in this regard. Over the last four-plus years, Ukraine has offered a vivid illustration that a middle power can confront a far greater one and avoid defeat. Despite Russiaâs overwhelming advantages in population, military-industrial capacity and nuclear status, Ukraine has not only resisted conquest since February 2022, but has imposed disproportionate costs on the aggressor, including long-range strikes deep inside Russian territory that have unsettled Moscowâs calculations and prompted the previously sceptical Donald Trump to change his stance on Kyivâs chances. While Ukraineâs resilience has depended on external support, its agency in whole-of-society mobilisation, drone-warfare innovation, and asymmetric strategy has been decisive. In the first weeks after the invasion, Poland became the main logistical corridor for western arms transfers, delivering some of Ukraineâs earliest heavy equipment. At the same time, Poland absorbed the largest share of Ukrainian refugees, funding reception and integration at a scale unmatched elsewhere. This response was driven not only by threat perception and humanitarian imperative, but it also demonstrated Polandâs ambition to assert regional leadership. The country positioned itself as a key player in shaping the Westâs response, providing lethal aid even before the invasion, and pressed larger western allies towards firmer positions. That early solidarity has since been reinforced by a genuine structural transformation: Polandâs defence budget has roughly tripled over the past decade, reaching the highest ratio in NATO â nearing five per cent of its GDP this year. The Polish armed forces have more than doubled since 2014, with plans to reach 300,000 personnel by 2035, making Poland the EUâs largest land force. The EUâs collective response serves as a good example of what middle powers can achieve by acting together. When the US sharply curtailed assistance to Ukraine in early 2025, European aid did not collapse. Funding channelled through EU institutions rose from roughly half of total European assistance in 2022 to nearly 90 percent by 2025, substituting for the American shortfall. The fact that a coalition of middle and small powers sustained Ukraineâs war effort without its largest former patron demonstrates that acting together, middle powers can substitute for the protection a single great power once provided. Great powers are also starting to recognise the growing influence of middle powers. Through much of 2025, President Trumpâs statements towards Ukraine were often dismissive, yet by mid-2026, following Ukrainian successes and the EUâs demonstrated capacity to sustain support independently, his rhetoric shifted. During this yearâs G7 and NATO summits, Trump had begun praising Ukraineâs resilience, aligning more closely with European positions. This shift should not be assumed irreversible, but it is consistent with a basic realist logic: demonstrated resolve and capability, not appeals for sympathy, alter a great powerâs calculus of respect. Ukraine's drone strikes against Russia. | Exilenova+ / screengrab A shared, secure future, not a contentious past The clearest emerging illustration of complementary middle-power roles is in missile and drone defence, where Ukrainian experience and Polish industrial capacity are becoming genuinely interlocking assets. Following Trumpâs announcement at the July 2026 NATO summit in Ankara that Washington would allow Ukraine to license-produce Patriot interceptor missiles, Poland proposed a trilateral framework with the US and Ukraine, under which production and maintenance would take place on Polish soil, drawing on an existing agreement Warsaw had signed with the US, Germany, the Netherlands and Sweden to host a European Patriot PAC-3 service centre. Polish officials have framed this explicitly as a way of combining Ukrainian operational knowledge with a secure, allied manufacturing base close to, but outside, the range of the heaviest Russian strikes, addressing both Kyivâs need for scale and Washingtonâs concerns about producing sensitive systems inside an active war zone. A parallel dynamic is underway in counter-drone defence. Ukraineâs forces have developed some of the worldâs most combat-tested methods for intercepting mass drone and missile salvoes, downing over a thousand Shahed-type drones with a reported roughly 95 percent success rate using low-cost interceptor systems. This expertise is highly valuable for Polandâs Eastern Shield programme and the broader European âdrone wallâ initiative launched with France, Germany, Italy and the UK after Russian drones repeatedly violated Polish and other allied airspace in 2025. Volodymyr Zelensky | AP Ukraineâs president, Volodymyr Zelensky, has explicitly offered to help Poland and other partners build âa joint, truly reliable shield against Russian aerial threatsâ, based on Ukraineâs battlefield experience, while Polish and Ukrainian manufacturers already cooperate on joint training and production projects. This critical cooperation, however, is being tested by an historical dispute which Europe can least afford at this moment. In mid-2026, a diplomatic crisis erupted after Zelensky renamed a military unit in honour of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) â commemorated in Ukraine as a symbol of resistance to Soviet domination, but remembered in Poland chiefly as the perpetrator of the 1943â44 mass killings of Polish civilians in Volhynia (WoÅyÅ) region. This moved was followed by the decision of the Polish president, Karol Nawrocki, to strip Zelensky of Polandâs highest state honour (which the previous president Andrzej Duda had awarded in 2023). This episode provides fertile ground for Russian influence campaigns to exploit growing anti-Ukrainian sentiment in Poland â sentiment already layered over the longer-running dispute over Ukrainian agricultural exports and EU accession terms. Ahead of Polandâs 2027 elections, these tensions risk complicating Ukraineâs membership process through bilateral âmemory politicsâ. This dispute is one that Europe cannot afford, given that no other European state could replace Polandâs role as NATOâs principal logistics hub for Ukraine in the foreseeable future. Ukraineâs continued resistance is equally crucial for Polish security on NATOâs eastern flank. Thankfully, both governments appear to have shown that they can step back from the brink: Zelenskyâs decision to open historical archives on the Volhynian tragedy and authorise broader exhumations, and quiet diplomacy between the two presidents at the Ankara NATO summit, suggest that the relationshipâs structural logic still outweighs its emotional politics. But this cannot be left to improvised de-escalation after each flare-up. Given how much depends on both countriesâ security, Poles and Ukrainians have a direct interest in quarrelling less over an unresolved and painful past and cooperating more deliberately around a common European future, treating historical reconciliation as a standing diplomatic project rather than a recurring source of crisis. European Union and Ukraine flags | AP Middle powers guarding Europeâs eastern flank Against the backdrop of Russiaâs war against Ukraine, the volatility of American policy under Trump, and the strengthening of authoritarian and illiberal tendencies globally, the EU has been compelled to demonstrate that an alliance of medium and small powers can be an equally strong actor. This does not require uniform contributions from every state, but rather a smart division of responsibilities and specialisations, within which countries apply their comparative advantages to promote shared European values, security, and prosperity. Ukraine and Poland have adjacent, mutually reinforcing niches within this division of responsibilities. Ukraine has become the EUâs frontline of defence with advanced experience in modern warfare, drone technology and societal resilience under existential pressure. Poland has established itself as the logistical and political hinge connecting that frontline to the rest of the EU, while rapidly building its own military-industrial base needed to convert battlefield lessons into deployable European capability. Their further strengthening and success as middle powers are crucial for Europe to achieve genuine strategic autonomy. What both governments and societies now owe each other, and the EU as a whole, is the discipline to keep that cooperation from being derailed by unresolved historical, political and even economic disputes, at precisely the moment when their own security and that of the whole of Europeâs eastern flank depends on getting it right. Maksym Khylko is the chairman at the East European Security Research Initiative, and Associate Professor at the Institute of European Studies and International Relations, Faculty of Social and Economic Sciences, Comenius University. Adam Reichardt is the editor-in-chief of New Eastern Europe and the co-host of the Talk Eastern Europe podcast and YouTube channel. LR

(Photo by Wojtek RADWANSKI / AFP) Content Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied Flip Smoked sausages and homemade cheese drew locals to a harvest festival in eastern Latvia – this time accompanied by campaign speeches from election candidates, including representatives of pro-Russian parties. But like the local produce, many members of the Russian-speaking minority in Rezekne, less than 50 kilometers (30 miles) from the Russian border, told AFP they identified with Latvia. JOIN US ON TELEGRAM Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official . A source of tension since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Latvia’s Russian-speaking community has faced renewed questions over identity, loyalty, and Moscow’s influence. As parliamentary elections loom on Oct. 3, many Russian speakers in the eastern Latgale region said they had no desire to be “saved” by Moscow. Advertisement “We do not need help from Russia here. We can solve our problems ourselves,” 45-year-old local resident Igors Nazarovs told AFP as a band played on the city’s main street. This is a separate culture – a separate land Russian President Vladimir Putin has repeatedly claimed that the rights of Russian speakers in the Baltic states are being violated, rhetoric that has raised concern in Latvia, Lithuania, and Estonia. His language has echoes of claims Moscow made about Russian speakers in Ukraine’s Donbas region before launching its invasion. Russian world Daugavpils, Latvia’s second-largest city, has around 80,000 residents, roughly 90% of whom are Russian-speaking. Other Topics of Interest Putin Envoy Talks Post-War Energy Deals as US Weighs Belarus-Style Sanctions Plan for Russia The Atlantic reports Washington is considering a model used with Minsk, where 25 prisoners were freed as sanctions on two Belarusian companies were lifted. Some Russian speakers there, including Inna Plavoka, said Russia’s war against Ukraine forced them to reconsider their own identity. When Russia launched its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, “my life was divided into a ‘before’ and an ‘after,’” she told AFP. “Today, I clearly identify with Latvia and with this country, in no way with Russia.” Plavoka, editor-in-chief of the independent Daugavpils media outlet Tchaika, or “Seagull,” said she believes a growing number of Russian speakers now feel the same way. Advertisement Before the war, she still knew people who believed Putin would come to Latvia “to save them” by offering them “Russki mir” – a phrase that can be translated as both “the Russian world” and “Russian peace.” Today, she said, she no longer knows anyone who openly says: “Yes, I want that.” Recent drone crashes on Latvian territory have also changed attitudes, she added. “Everyone understands what this ‘Russki mir’ really means.” Portraits of Lenin and Stalin Affection for Moscow, however, remains among some older members of Latvia’s Russian-speaking population. At the offices of the Latvian Russian Community association, Aleksei Vassiliev, a candidate from the Russian-speaking Harmony party, proudly pointed to portraits of Soviet leaders Vladimir Lenin and Joseph Stalin. “This is the history of people who lived in the Soviet Union,” he said. While insisting that he is attached to Latvia, Vassiliev criticized the status of so-called “non-citizens” – permanent residents, mostly Russian-speaking, who did not meet the full requirements for Latvian citizenship and hold no other nationality. Advertisement Many either failed or did not take the Latvian language and history examinations required for citizenship. They make up nearly 9% of Latvia’s population and are not permitted to vote. “If they were allowed to vote and if they voted as a bloc, they would be the largest parliamentary group in parliament,” Vassiliev said. He also criticized measures adopted by Riga since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine aimed at reducing Russian influence, including the transition toward Latvian as the main language of instruction and the removal of Soviet monuments. Kremlin influence and economic frustration In Latgale, the poorest region of the Baltic states, some Russian-speaking residents also criticize European support for Ukraine. Their complaints often appear rooted more in local economic hardship than in direct support for the Kremlin. Seeking votes from that electorate, Vjaceslavs Stepanenko, leader of the local branch of the populist Suverena Vara party – accused by critics of pro-Russian sympathies – attacked European assistance to Kyiv. “It would be nice if this aid from European countries were for us,” he said. Only a few meters away, center-right MP Juris Vilums of the United List handed out his own campaign leaflets. Led by Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs, the party is leading in opinion polls and is expected to play a central role in forming Latvia’s next governing coalition, while maintaining the country’s broadly centrist and pro-Western course. Advertisement Vilums argued that Russian influence persists in parts of eastern Latvia largely because local residents lack alternative sources of information. “The major problem... is propaganda,” he said. “For now, we don’t have any Russian-language media at the national level,” Vilums added, noting that residents near the border can easily receive Russian or Belarusian radio broadcasts. While one part of Latvia’s Russian-speaking population “is already integrated,” he said, “another part is not, and I’m afraid it never will be.” To suggest a correction or clarification, write to us here You can also highlight the text and press Ctrl + Enter Contact Us Please leave your suggestions or corrections here Cancel Send AFP POPULAR Did Ukraine Use Pelican Ballistic Missile to Strike Moscow? https://www.dw.com/en/uganda-says-it-has.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OaQW Both patients are known to have traveled through Uganda's Entebbe International Airport on October 3 Image: Sumy Sadurni/AFP/Getty Images Advertisement The first confirmed Ebola patients in Kenya and Nigeria may have crossed paths at Uganda's Entebbe International Airport, according to African health officials, as new information from Switzerland contradicts Uganda's account of the Nigerian patient's travel history. Uganda , a country reporting no active Ebola infections, has become a focus of investigations into cases thousands of kilometers apart. Uganda insists it has no confirmed active cases of the deadly virus . Yet health authorities in Kenya and Nigeria are investigating Ebola infections involving people whose travel histories or contacts are connected to the East African nation. Both patients passed through Entebbe International Airport on October 3, according to Wessam Mankoula, head of emergency preparedness and response at the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) . Health officials say the two may have crossed paths, although it has not been established whether they encountered each other or whether any transmission occurred at the airport. The differing accounts have raised questions about whether Uganda was simply a transit point for infected travelers, or could infections be going undetected along some of Africa's busiest cross-border routes? The latest developments come after Switzerland disputed claims that the Nigerian patient had visited the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) , where an Ebola outbreak is underway. Did the two Ebola patients cross paths in Uganda? Nigeria's Health Minister Muhammad Ali Pate confirmed an imported Ebola case in the Nigerian capital, Abuja , involving a woman who had recently traveled to East Africa, including Uganda. "Today we are confirming that there has been one imported case of Ebola virus disease in the Federal Capital Territory," Pate said. The woman developed symptoms on October 7 and visited a private health facility on October 11. Further laboratory testing confirmed Ebola, and she was subsequently isolated for treatment. Pate said the patient was stable and that health officials had identified 44 contacts, including healthcare workers, caregivers, patients and people who may have encountered her during her travels. But the woman's journey has become central to the investigation. Speaking on Thursday, Mankoula said the first confirmed patients in Kenya and Nigeria were both known to have traveled through Entebbe International Airport on October 3. Investigators are examining whether the two patients were at the airport at the same time and whether their movements overlapped. Switzerland contradicts Uganda's account Uganda's Health Ministry says preliminary findings indicate the Nigerian patient traveled to eastern DRC for business before passing through Uganda without symptoms and returning to Nigeria. "Travel through Uganda does not establish that infection occurred here. The location of exposure remains under investigation," the ministry said in an October 20 statement. But on Friday, Switzerland's Federal Department of Foreign Affairs directly disputed the account. "She and her husband did not travel to the Democratic Republic of the Congo," the department said in a statement to Reuters news agency. The woman, identified by Swiss authorities as a Swiss national of Ugandan origin, is married to a Swiss diplomat based in Abuja. Ebola cases have now been detected in four African countries: DR Congo, ​Uganda, Kenya ‌and Nigeria Image: Afolabi Sotunde/AP Photo/picture alliance On Thursday, the Swiss government told Reuters that she was believed to have contracted Ebola while traveling with her husband in Uganda, although that assessment has not been independently confirmed. The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Africa CDC also said Thursday that they had not received confirmed information establishing that the woman had traveled to the DRC. The conflicting accounts raise fresh questions about where the woman was exposed to the virus and how accurately her movements were initially reconstructed. They do not, however, establish that she contracted Ebola in Uganda. Uganda maintains it has no confirmed active Ebola cases and says it is awaiting more detailed information from Nigeria about the woman's movements. Kenya's missing contact complicates investigation In Kenya, Uganda has emerged in a separate investigation involving the country's first confirmed Ebola patient, who died in the Kenyan capital, Nairobi, on October 5. The patient had traveled from the Democratic Republic of Congo through Uganda before reaching Kenya. Health officials have now established that the patient passed through Entebbe International Airport on October 3, the same day as the woman subsequently diagnosed in Nigeria. Kenyan authorities have since reported additional infections linked to the initial case. But one aspect of the investigation remains unresolved. According to Kenya's Daily Nation , health officials are searching for a Ugandan national identified as a contact of the deceased patient. "We know him (the Ugandan) by name and passport number and from his phone but we are not able to reach him," Kenya's Director-General for Health Patrick Amoth told the newspaper. The Daily Nation reported that the man was using a South Sudanese telephone number, complicating efforts to establish his whereabouts. Being an untraced contact does not mean he is infected. However, locating potentially exposed individuals is essential to preventing further transmission. Can border screening stop Ebola? Uganda shares a lengthy border with the Democratic Republic of Congo, where Ebola outbreaks have repeatedly challenged health authorities. Cross-border trade, population movements and international travel make it difficult to establish where someone was exposed to the virus. According to the WHO, people infected with Ebola are not considered infectious until symptoms appear. Even well-functioning border surveillance systems cannot identify every infected traveler. The discovery that both patients traveled through the same international airport on the same day illustrates the complexity of tracing potential exposures across multiple countries. It also highlights the importance of reconstructing travel histories and identifying close contacts. Uganda says it is strengthening screening and public health controls at points of entry, while Nigeria has intensified contact tracing and infection prevention measures. The challenge is ensuring that authorities across different countries can exchange accurate information quickly enough to identify potential exposures. Anxiety grows in Nigeria In Abuja, the confirmed infection has revived memories of previous Ebola outbreaks. Resident Peace Kolawole expressed concern about the consequences of another outbreak. "So here is my hand sanitizer, so I'm actually very concerned about it," she told DW. Others fear Nigeria's healthcare system may struggle to respond while many citizens face economic hardship. "Because now people are not even worried about sickness anymore, people are worried about surviving," Abuja resident Jonathan Steven told DW. Nigeria's health authorities say the patient is receiving medical care and that contact tracing is continuing. What remains unanswered? Uganda's position between the DRC and other regional destinations offers one explanation for its appearance in both investigations. But the latest findings have added two significant questions: Did the patients from Kenya and Nigeria come into contact at Entebbe International Airport on October 3, and where did the Nigerian woman contract the virus if, as Switzerland insists, she never traveled to DR Congo? Did Ebola start spreading before officials even knew? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The conflicting accounts from Uganda and Switzerland have made establishing the Nigerian patient's travel history an urgent part of the investigation. The WHO and Africa CDC have yet to confirm the disputed DR Congo travel history. Uganda's declaration of zero confirmed active cases does not establish that all infections have been ruled out. Equally, the travel histories do not prove an undetected outbreak. For Kenya and Nigeria, the immediate priority is containing confirmed infections. For Uganda, the challenge is demonstrating that its surveillance systems are effective and reassuring both its citizens and neighboring countries. The Africa CDC will convene an "extraordinary virtual meeting" of national health officials on October 28 as the continent's latest Ebola outbreak continues to spread.
